title: Pagosa Springs Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Pagosa Springs wells have a 150 ft median depth, 9 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $15,800-$27,000.
intro_html: Rural property around Pagosa Springs commonly depends on private wells completed in mountain bedrock. The local permit record shows a 150-foot median well depth and a 9.0-gpm median reported yield, but the range is wide. Some wells are shallow; others reach far deeper in fractured rock. Use these figures to screen a property, compare neighboring wells, and ask a driller for a site-specific opinion before buying or building.

sections.heading: Pagosa Springs well depths vary with the mountain geology
sections.html:
Among wells with reported total depth, the median is 150 feet. The middle half runs from 64 to 280 feet, so a typical drilling bid needs to allow for meaningful variation even within the same general area. The 90th-percentile depth is 391 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,465 feet.

The depth mix gives a useful first look: 35% are under 100 feet, 42% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 19% from 300 to 600 feet, and 4% exceed 600 feet. Permits most often name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. In granite and gneiss, water follows fractures rather than a uniform underground layer, so nearby depth is helpful context, not a guarantee for your lot.

sections.heading: What Pagosa Springs wells produce
sections.html:
Reported well yield has a 9.0-gpm median, with the middle half between 5.0 and 14.0 gpm. Sixty percent of reported yields are in the 5-to-15-gpm range, while 25% report more than 15 gpm. At the low end, 6% are under 1 gpm and another 9% fall between 1 and 5 gpm.

That low-yield share matters to a buyer. A well making less than 1 gpm may still serve a carefully managed household with storage, but it offers less margin for irrigation, guests, leaks, or future expansion. Ask for the well construction report and a current pump test. A permit record reports what was documented at the time; it does not replace testing the actual well and pressure system.

sections.heading: Pagosa Springs water levels are unevenly documented
sections.html:
The recorded static water level has a 28-foot median, with the middle half from 5 to 145 feet below ground. That spread is large enough to affect pump installation, storage, and the cost of bringing water into a house. It also shows why one neighbor’s shallow water level should not be treated as a promise for another parcel.

Only 10 wells report a static water level, so this data set is too small to establish a reliable water-table trend by decade. The available records cannot support a conclusion that groundwater is generally dropping or rising around Pagosa Springs. Have the driller check nearby logs, confirm the proposed well location, and measure the completed well after construction.

sections.heading: A long permit history, with several recurring drillers
sections.html:
Pagosa Springs has a substantial well record: 699 wells appear in Colorado DWR permit records, 364 are recorded as constructed, 400 report total depth, and 101 report pump yield. Permits were issued in every decade shown, with the largest group in the 1970s at 177. The record also includes 21 permits from the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2025.

The most active drillers in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 72 wells; Smith Water Well Service (Sanders, O L), with 66; and Beeman Bros Drilling Inc (Beeman, J. L.), with 63. Those names help when tracing nearby construction histories. Confirm current licensing, availability, and scope directly, and have a Colorado DWR professional review the permit file for the parcel you are considering.

sections.heading: Estimated drilling cost around Pagosa Springs
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, at about $65-$100 per foot. At the 150-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models to roughly $9,800-$15,000. A finished well including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $15,800-$27,000.

These figures are planning ranges, not a fixed bid. Depth is the largest unknown, and hard fractured rock can change drilling time and completion requirements. A quote should state the assumed depth, casing and grout, pump equipment, water line, electrical work, testing, and what happens if the hole is dry or produces too little water. Compare bids on the same scope rather than on footage alone.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Low yield and dry holes are the main geology-related concerns in fractured mountain bedrock. The records show 6% of reported yields under 1 gpm, so ask specifically about the weakest nearby wells, not only the median. A well can also make water at completion but have a pump, storage, or pressure-system problem that affects usable supply.

Environmental review matters too. Within about 10 miles, the map includes 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the mapped facts, but that does not make every private well automatically safe. Test for contaminants appropriate to the property and local setting. Before construction, confirm septic setbacks, soil suitability, well access, and the location of the house, driveway, and drainfield.

sections.heading: A practical Pagosa Springs lot review
sections.html:
For a property near Pagosa Springs, start with the Colorado DWR permit and construction records for the parcel and nearby wells. Compare depths, reported yields, static levels, aquifer names, and construction details. Nearby areas such as Arboles, Bayfield, South Fork, Southern Ute, and Ignacio may provide broader regional context, but they are not substitutes for records close to the lot.

Before closing, make the purchase decision depend on usable water, not just an existing permit. Inspect the pump and pressure equipment, obtain a current flow or recovery test, and test the water. For a vacant lot, get a driller’s siting opinion and a septic evaluation before finalizing a house plan. Confirm access for a large rig, power availability, storage needs, and any augmentation or water-right requirements that apply to the proposed use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Pagosa Springs?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Pagosa Springs is 150 feet. The middle half runs from 64 to 280 feet, 19% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 4% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,465 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes neighboring well depth useful for planning, but not a guarantee for a new lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Pagosa Springs?
faq.a: The local model uses $65-$100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 150-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $9,800-$15,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $15,800-$27,000. Actual bids depend on depth, access, construction requirements, and the final equipment scope.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Pagosa Springs?
faq.a: Reported yield has a 9.0-gpm median, with the middle half from 5.0 to 14.0 gpm. Sixty percent of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gpm, while 6% are under 1 gpm. Ask for a pump test and recovery information, because a permit’s reported yield does not guarantee current household performance.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Pagosa Springs?
faq.a: A permit record cannot establish that a private well is safe to drink. The mapped area includes 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 historic mine features within about 10 miles. Test the property’s water for contaminants appropriate to its location and history. Also inspect the wellhead, casing, grout, pressure system, and septic layout.

faq.q: Do Pagosa Springs wells have a falling water table?
faq.a: The available records do not show a reliable trend. Only 10 wells report static water level, with a median depth to water of 28 feet and a middle half from 5 to 145 feet. That sample is too limited to conclude that groundwater is generally falling or rising. A driller should review nearby logs and measure the completed well.
